lesson.title: Knocking Electrons Loose: Einstein's Photoelectric Effect
lesson.summary: When light of sufficient energy strikes a metal, it ejects electrons instantly, a result that only makes sense if light truly is made of discrete photons, and it earned Einstein his Nobel Prize.
lesson.body:
By the late 1800s, physicists knew that shining light on certain metal surfaces could eject electrons, a phenomenon called the photoelectric effect. Classical wave theory made a clear prediction: since a wave's energy depends on its intensity (brightness), even dim light should eventually eject electrons if you shine it long enough for energy to accumulate, and brighter light should always eject electrons with more kinetic energy. Experiments showed the opposite. Below a certain threshold frequency, no electrons were ejected no matter how bright or how long the light shone. Above that threshold, electrons popped out instantly, and their kinetic energy depended only on the frequency of the light, not its intensity. Something was fundamentally wrong with the wave picture.

Einstein resolved the puzzle in 1905 by taking Planck's quantum idea seriously as a description of light itself, not just a mathematical trick for blackbody radiation. He proposed that light striking the metal arrives as individual photons, each carrying energy E = hf. A single photon transfers its entire energy to a single electron in one instant, all or nothing. If that energy exceeds the work function, phi, the minimum energy needed to pull an electron free of the metal, the electron escapes, and any energy left over becomes its kinetic energy: KE_max = hf - phi. If the photon energy is less than phi, the electron simply cannot escape, regardless of how many such photons arrive.

Sodium metal has a work function of about 2.28 eV. Suppose we illuminate it with blue light at 400 nm. Its frequency is f = c / lambda = (3.00 x 10^8 m/s) / (400 x 10^-9 m) = 7.50 x 10^14 Hz, and the photon energy is E = hf = (6.626 x 10^-34)(7.50 x 10^14) = 4.97 x 10^-19 J, or about 3.10 eV. Since 3.10 eV exceeds the 2.28 eV work function, electrons are ejected, and each carries a maximum kinetic energy of KE_max = 3.10 eV - 2.28 eV = 0.82 eV. Notice this calculation never used how bright the light was, only its wavelength.

Brightness still matters, just not for kinetic energy. A brighter beam simply means more photons arriving per second, so more electrons get ejected per second (a larger photoelectric current), but each individual electron still leaves with the same maximum kinetic energy set by the frequency. Every metal has its own threshold frequency, f0 = phi / h, below which even an intense beam of low-frequency light ejects nothing. For sodium, f0 works out to about 5.51 x 10^14 Hz, corresponding to a wavelength near 544 nm, in the green part of the visible spectrum; red light, with a lower frequency than that, cannot eject electrons from sodium no matter how powerful the laser.

This all-or-nothing, frequency-dependent behavior is exactly what a continuous wave cannot produce but a stream of discrete photons explains perfectly, and it is why Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics specifically for explaining the photoelectric effect rather than for relativity. The same bookkeeping, photon energy in, binding energy subtracted, kinetic energy out, reappears almost unchanged in photoelectron spectroscopy, where higher energy photons eject electrons from gas-phase atoms to probe how tightly each electron is held.
